newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn seen near post monopoly compromise.
newsitem.headline: Bonn seen near post monopoly compromise.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition could be close to a compromise on restricting the letter monopoly of the post office, government coalition sources said on Monday.

The sources said Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and his junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) had agreed to grant Deutsche Post AG a monopoly for up to five years on letters weighing up to 100 grams.
That is well below the 350 grams originally supported by Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch and reflects the influence of the free market forces in the FDP.
Post Ministry State Secretary Gerhard Pfeffermann said Boetsch had signalled that a 100 gram limit would be an acceptable compromise.
The sources, who declined to be named, said a decision had yet to be reached on whether the licence should last for four or five years before full competition.

Boetsch told German radio on Monday that full competition for parcels should be started on January 1, 1998, but said the post office should keep its monopoly on letters under 350 grams for a five-year transition period.
He said he wanted the post office to maintain its monopoly in this area because of the costs of getting the post office, which became Deutsche Post AG in 1995, ready for competition.
If the monopoly was not maintained beyond 1998 then large job losses would result and the tax payer would have to bear the burden of redundancy costs, he said.

The Bonn government is due to discuss on Tuesday a draft law that would sweep aside the centuries-old monopoly set up by the Thurn and Taxis aristocracy which laid the basis for modern postal delivery in the 17th century.
Meanwhile, more than 20,000 German postal workers converged in a convoy of buses on Bonn to protest against the plans.
